blocks.text: A plate of jollof rice, a piece of grilled tilapia and a bowl of egusi soup all store sunlight that a green plant trapped weeks or months ago. Follow any mouthful backwards: rice plant to grain to you; phytoplankton to tilapia to you; melon leaf to caterpillar to hen to you. That trail is a food chain, and at every step most of the energy leaks away as heat.

blocks.markdown:
## Food chains and trophic levels

A **food chain** is a linear sequence showing who eats whom, with arrows pointing in the direction of energy flow.

A Nigerian farm example:

maize → grasshopper → toad → snake → hawk

A mangrove creek example:

mangrove leaf fragments → crab → tilapia → heron

Each step is a **trophic level**:

- **Producer** (first trophic level): a green plant or alga that makes food by photosynthesis.
- **Primary consumer** (second trophic level): a herbivore that eats the producer.
- **Secondary consumer** (third trophic level): a carnivore that eats the herbivore.
- **Tertiary consumer** (fourth trophic level): a carnivore that eats other carnivores.

A **food web** is several food chains linked together, because most animals eat more than one thing and are themselves eaten by more than one predator. **Decomposers** — bacteria and fungi — break down dead bodies and waste at every trophic level and are usually drawn to the side of the web rather than as one extra link.

blocks.title: Trophic level
blocks.text: The feeding position of an organism in a food chain. Producers occupy level 1, herbivores level 2, and successive carnivores occupy levels 3, 4 and so on. An omnivore such as a human can occupy more than one trophic level in the same web.

blocks.markdown:
## Why energy decreases along a food chain

Only about **10%** of the energy stored at one trophic level is transferred to the next. The rest is lost because:

- much of the organism is never eaten (bones, wood, roots);
- some of what is eaten is egested as faeces;
- a large fraction is used in **respiration** and leaves the chain as **heat**.

That is why food chains are short — usually four or five links at most — and why a hectare of maize can feed far more people if they eat the grain than if they first feed it to goats and then eat the meat. Energy for the whole chain originally comes from the sun, trapped by producers.

**Pyramids** display this pattern. A **pyramid of numbers** counts individuals at each level. A **pyramid of biomass** weighs the living material. A **pyramid of energy** shows energy flowing through each level per unit time. The pyramid of energy is **always upright**, because energy is lost at every transfer and cannot increase up the chain.

items: A pyramid of numbers is often upright (many grasses, fewer grasshoppers, still fewer toads), but it can be inverted: one mango tree may support thousands of caterpillars.
A pyramid of biomass is usually upright. It can invert briefly in a pond, where a small standing crop of fast-reproducing phytoplankton supports a larger mass of zooplankton.
A pyramid of energy cannot invert. Heat loss from respiration makes each level smaller than the one below it.
Decomposers recycle nutrients but do not restore the energy already lost as heat; only photosynthesis brings new energy in.

blocks.title: Interpreting an inverted pyramid of numbers
blocks.prompt: A student counts organisms on one mango tree in a compound: 1 tree, 8 000 caterpillars, 200 parasitic wasps that lay eggs in the caterpillars. Sketch the pyramid of numbers, name each trophic level, and explain whether a pyramid of energy for the same system could have the same shape.

steps.text: The producer is a single large tree, so the base of the numbers pyramid is a narrow bar of 1.
The primary consumers are the 8 000 caterpillars, so the second bar is much wider — the pyramid is inverted at this step.
The secondary consumers are the 200 wasps, so the third bar is narrower than the caterpillar bar but still wider than the tree.

Energy, however, must decrease at each transfer. The tree's annual energy capture is far greater than the energy in the caterpillars, which is greater than the energy in the wasps. A pyramid of energy for the same chain is therefore upright even though the numbers pyramid is inverted.

blocks.answer: Numbers: inverted (1 tree → many caterpillars → fewer wasps). Energy: always upright, because only about 10% of the energy passes to the next level and the rest is lost as heat.

blocks.title: WAEC and JAMB tip
blocks.text: Arrows in a food chain show the direction of energy flow, not 'is eaten by' written the wrong way. If a question shows an inverted pyramid, first ask whether it is numbers (possible) or energy (impossible). Naming decomposers as a trophic level in the chain itself is a common way to lose a mark — they act on all levels.

points: A food chain is producer → primary consumer → secondary consumer → tertiary consumer; arrows point towards the eater, showing energy flow.
A food web is interconnected chains; decomposers recycle dead material at every level.
Only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level reaches the next; the rest is lost as heat from respiration, as uneaten parts and as faeces.
Pyramids of numbers and biomass can invert; a pyramid of energy is always upright.
Short chains and eating producers rather than meat transfer more of the original sunlight to humans.
